report.summary: Token-based (CCFinder, SourcererCC) recall >90%, precision ~60-70%; tree-based Deckard recall 90%, precision ~75-90%; semantic Oreo uncertain. Only incremental token-based (iClones) is cheap per commit.

handoff.full_answer: CCFinder (Kamiya et al., 2002) uses a suffix-tree token-based approach. Evaluated on large systems (JDK, Linux), it detected many clones but manual inspection revealed false positives from normalized identifiers; precision estimated 70–80%, recall high (>90%) as it misses few Type-1/2 clones. SourcererCC (Sajnani et al., 2016) token-based with bag-of-tokens and filtering, reporting on BigCloneBench: recall 99% for Type-1/2, 93% for Type-3 clones with precision 62%. After post-filtering, precision rises to 96% while recall drops to 87%. Tree-based Deckard (Jiang et al., 2007) uses AST and LSH to cluster similar subtrees; precision-recall tradeoff: at recall 0.9, precision is 0.76; at recall 0.8, precision reaches 0.9. Deckard outperforms CCFinder in precision for similar recall. Oreo (uncertain; possibly a GNN-based semantic detector) claims semantic clone detection but reliable benchmarks are scarce; other semantic tools like ASTNN often achieve recall >90% but precision ~50–70% and require GPU resources, making them unsuitable for per-commit usage. For per-commit integration, the only viable approach is a fast incremental token-based detector. iClones (Göde and Koschke, 2009) exactly addresses this: it incrementally updates token sequences from diffs, achieving sub-second detection on typical commits while maintaining recall comparable to full scans. Setting a high similarity threshold or applying SourcererCC's post-filter can boost precision to avoid developer alarm fatigue. Adopt incremental token-based clone detection, with optional conservative filtering, as a commit-time quality gate.
